context: You will hear part of a lecture about urban heat islands.

script.t: Today's lecture is about urban heat islands, which is the term used to describe cities that are significantly warmer than the countryside around them.

The difference can be surprisingly large. On a calm summer night, the centre of a large city can be up to 10 degrees Celsius warmer than nearby rural areas. The effect is usually strongest at night rather than during the day.
There are several causes. The first is the materials cities are built from. Asphalt and concrete absorb heat from the sun during the day and release it slowly after dark.

The second cause is the lack of vegetation. In the countryside, plants cool the air through a process called evapotranspiration, in which water evaporates from their leaves. Cities, with far fewer plants, lose much of this natural cooling.
Third, the shape of cities matters. Tall buildings close together create what are sometimes called urban canyons, which trap heat and reduce wind.
And finally, human activity itself produces heat: from cars, factories and, ironically, air conditioners, which pump hot air out into the street.
Why does this matter? The most serious consequence is for health. During heatwaves, death rates rise sharply, and elderly people are most at risk.

Higher temperatures also increase energy use, as more people switch on air conditioning, and they can worsen air quality, because heat speeds up the chemical reactions that produce ground-level ozone.

So what can be done? One of the simplest solutions is to make surfaces lighter in colour. Los Angeles, for example, has experimented with coating streets in a light grey material that reflects sunlight, and measurements suggest these streets can be several degrees cooler.
Green roofs, which are covered with plants, are another option. They not only cool buildings but also absorb rainwater. However, they are expensive to install and require regular maintenance.

Finally, and perhaps most effectively, cities can plant more trees. Medellín in Colombia created a network of green corridors along roads and waterways, and temperatures along them fell by around 2 degrees.
